lesson_title: Snow in a Glass: Ions, Electrolytes and Precipitates
hook_text: Pour one clear liquid into another clear liquid — and SNOW appears. Solid, from two liquids. Here's the chemistry trick.
clip_script: Take two glasses of perfectly clear liquid — silver nitrate solution and salt solution. Pour one into the other. The instant they touch, white snow appears in the water, swirling and settling. No magic: a partner swap. Each glass was a crowd of swimming ions. Mixed together, silver ions met chloride ions — and that particular couple cannot swim. Silver chloride is insoluble, so every silver-chloride meeting welds solid, and the solid snows out. Chemists call the snow a precipitate — and once you can force snow on demand, you can use it to name an invisible ion hiding in any mystery bottle.
visual_style: Macro shot of two clear glasses pouring together with an instant white snowfall; cut to a particle view of ion crowds mingling and the silver-chloride couples locking solid and sinking.
mood: Magic-trick wonder resolved into detective satisfaction.
pacing: Slow pour, sudden snowfall beat, brisk particle-level explanation, teasing close on the mystery bottle.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn the ion test kit — acid, silver, barium — like a lab detective.
